No. 

While the story contains a few brief visual and auditory details—such as coffee "the color of dishwater," a town "the color of a bruise," a water stain "shaped like the state of Maine," and a radiator that "clicked like a metronome"—it largely lacks rich sensory descriptions. There are no descriptions of smells or tastes (even when the characters order lamb at a restaurant or drink coffee), and very little engagement with physical textures or temperatures. Instead, the writer focuses almost entirely on internal monologue, emotional states, and psychological observations rather than building a tangible, sensory-rich physical environment.
